facts: $\mathrm{CG}^{\mathrm{ns}} \le \mathrm{CG}^{*} \le \mathrm{CG}^{\mathrm{pub}} \le \mathrm{CG}$. Private coin is the one variant of the four that escapes the collapse to the classical adversary bound [CGLMSG23].

The sandwich: $\max\{\mathrm{Adv}(f)^2,\ \mathrm{R}_0(f),\ \mathrm{CA}(f)\} \le \mathrm{CG}(f) \le \min\{\mathrm{C}^0(f)\,\mathrm{C}^1(f),\ O(\mathrm{EC}(f)^2)\}$ [CGLMSG23, Thm 5.10]. For total $f$. The definition itself is stated for possibly-partial $f$, but the sandwich is not: the certificate-product bound needs a $0$-certificate and a $1$-certificate to conflict, and on a promise problem the input stitched together from two non-conflicting certificates may simply be outside the domain. It fails badly there -- \(\mathrm{WT}_n\) has $\mathrm{C} = \Theta(1)$ and $\mathrm{R}_0 = 2^{\Omega(n)}$, so no bound of the form $\mathrm{R}_0 \le \mathrm{CG} \le \mathrm{C}^0\mathrm{C}^1$ can survive.

The upper bound $\mathrm{CG}(f) \le \mathrm{C}^0(f)\,\mathrm{C}^1(f)$ is one line: each player outputs a uniformly random index of a minimal certificate for their own input, and a $0$-certificate and a $1$-certificate must conflict somewhere. It is tight for $\mathrm{OR}$ and for $\oplus$.

$\mathrm{CG}$ is not bounded by $\mathrm{D}$: it can exceed the arity of the function. $\mathrm{CG}(\oplus_n) = \Theta(n^2)$, because $\mathrm{C}^0\mathrm{C}^1 = n^2$ above and $\mathrm{Adv}(\oplus_n)^2 = n^2$ below.

The single-bit private-coin variant (inputs at Hamming distance $1$) equals $\lambda(f)^2$ [CGLMSG23, Thm 8.9]; the single-bit public-coin variant is $\Theta(\mathrm{s}(f))$ [CGLMSG23, Thm 8.4]. Since restricting the adversary to distance-$1$ pairs can only help the players, these are lower bounds on the unrestricted games.

other_lo.note:
Deutsch--Jozsa is the cleanest witness.  **Public coin:** both players output
one shared uniformly random index; a constant input and a balanced input differ
on $N/2$ of the $N$ positions, so this wins with probability $1/2$ and
$\mathrm{CG}^{\mathrm{pub}} \le 2$.  **Private coin:** pin Alice at $x = 0^N$,
where she has a single output distribution $p$ over $[N]$.  Let $S$ be the
$N/2$ indices on which $p$ is smallest, so $\max_{i \in S} p_i \le 2/N$, and let
Bob hold the balanced $y = \mathbf{1}_S$.  Whatever distribution Bob plays, the
win probability $\sum_{i \in S} p_i q_i$ is at most $\max_{i \in S} p_i \le 2/N$.
Hence $\mathrm{CG} \ge N/2$, and the matching strategy (both players uniform)
gives $\mathrm{CG} \le 2N$.

partial:
\(On promise problems the private-coin game is unboundedly harder than the public-coin one.\) partial No bound exists #

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{CG}(\mathrm{DJ}_N) = \Theta(N) \text{ while } \mathrm{CG}^{\mathrm{pub}}(\mathrm{DJ}_N) = \Theta(1)\)
    putative witness: \(\mathrm{DJ}_n\)
    Deutsch--Jozsa is the cleanest witness. Public coin: both players output one shared uniformly random index; a constant input and a balanced input differ on $N/2$ of the $N$ positions, so this wins with probability $1/2$ and $\mathrm{CG}^{\mathrm{pub}} \le 2$. Private coin: pin Alice at $x = 0^N$, where she has a single output distribution $p$ over $[N]$. Let $S$ be the $N/2$ indices on which $p$ is smallest, so $\max_{i \in S} p_i \le 2/N$, and let Bob hold the balanced $y = \mathbf{1}_S$. Whatever distribution Bob plays, the win probability $\sum_{i \in S} p_i q_i$ is at most $\max_{i \in S} p_i \le 2/N$. Hence $\mathrm{CG} \ge N/2$, and the matching strategy (both players uniform) gives $\mathrm{CG} \le 2N$.

Shared randomness is exactly what lets the two players agree on where to look, and on a promise problem there is nothing else forcing them to agree: the certificate-conflict argument that pins $\mathrm{CG}$ near $\mathrm{CG}^{\mathrm{pub}}$ for total $f$ needs the stitched-together input to be in the domain. For total $f$ the question is open -- no total family is known on which $\mathrm{CG}$ exceeds $\mathrm{CG}^{\mathrm{pub}}$ by more than a square, and $\oplus$ realises that square.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{CG}(f) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{Adv}(f)^2\big)\)
    CGLMSG23
    Theorem 5.10 of [CGLMSG23]: $\mathrm{CG}(f) \ge \mathrm{MM}(f)^2$, where $\mathrm{MM}$ is the minimax formulation of the positive adversary bound, itself sitting between $\lambda(f)$ and $\mathrm{Q}(f)$. Specialising to the Hamming-distance-$1$ game recovers the exact identity $\mathrm{CG}_{[1]}(f) = \lambda(f)^2$ [CGLMSG23, Thm 8.9]. This is what lets $\mathrm{CG}$ climb above the arity: $\mathrm{Adv}(\oplus_n) = n$ forces $\mathrm{CG}(\oplus_n) = \Omega(n^2)$.

No upper bound on $\mathrm{CG}$ in terms of $\mathrm{Adv}$ is known, and none should be expected in general: $\mathrm{CG}$ is also above $\mathrm{R}_0$, while $\mathrm{Adv}$ is below $\mathrm{Q}$. Any total function with a large $\mathrm{R}_0$-vs-$\mathrm{Q}$ gap therefore pushes the two apart -- $\mathrm{OR}_n$ already gives $\mathrm{CG} = \Theta(n)$ against $\mathrm{Adv} = \Theta(\sqrt n)$, which is exactly the tight case of the bound above rather than a separation. A genuine separation would need $\mathrm{CG} \gg \mathrm{Adv}^2$.
